metadata.title: On weight initialization in deep neural networks

nodes.name: Weight initialization variance problem
nodes.statement: The problem can be stated as follows: If the weights in a neural network are initialized using samples from a normal distribution, ${\cal{N}}(0,v^{2})$, how should $v^{2}$ be chosen to ensure that the variance of the outputs from the different layers are approximately the same?
nodes.statement_short: Choose the variance $v^2$ of normal weight initialization so all layer outputs have about the same variance.

nodes.name: Glorot-Bengio initialization for linear activations
nodes.statement: The first systematic analysis of this problem was conducted by Glorot and Bengio \cite{glorot2010understanding} who showed that for a linear activation function, the optimal value of $v^{2} = 1/N$, where $N$ is the number of nodes feeding into that layer.
assumptions: $N$ is the number of nodes feeding into that layer
nodes.statement_short: For linear activations the optimal weight variance is $1/N$ with $N$ the fan-in.

nodes.name: Xavier initialization
nodes.statement: Although the paper makes several assumptions about the inputs to the model, it works extremely well in many cases and is widely used in the initialization of neural networks to date; this initialization scheme is commonly referred to as the {\it{Xavier initialization}}.
nodes.statement_short: The $v^2=1/N$ scheme of Glorot and Bengio is called the Xavier initialization.

nodes.name: He initialization
nodes.statement: In an important follow up paper, He and colleagues \cite{he2015delving} argue that the {\it{Xavier initialization}} does not work well with the RELU activation function, and instead propose an initialization of $v^{2} = 2/N$ (commonly referred to as the {\it{He initialization}}).
nodes.statement_short: He et al. propose $v^2=2/N$ for RELU networks, called the He initialization.

nodes.name: Why Xavier fails and He succeeds for the 30-layer RELU network
nodes.statement: In support of their initialization, they provide an example of a 30 layer neural network which converges with the {\it{He initialization}}, but not under the {\it{Xavier initialization}}. To the best of my knowledge, the precise reason for the convergence of one method and the non-convergence of the other is not fully understood.
nodes.statement_short: Why the 30-layer RELU network converges with He but not with Xavier initialization was not understood.

nodes.name: Deep neural network with $M$ layers
nodes.statement: Consider a deep neural network with $M$ layers.

nodes.name: Layer recursions of a deep neural network
nodes.statement: The relationship between the inputs to the $m^{th}$ layer ($x_{m}$) and $m+1^{th}$ layer ($x_{m+1}$) are described by the recursions \begin{equation} y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N}{\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij} \enum{in1} \end{equation} and \begin{equation} x_{m+1}(i) = \mbox{g}(y_{m}(i)). \enum{in2} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Layer $m$ maps inputs $x_m$ to pre-activations $y_m=W_m x_m$ and outputs $x_{m+1}=g(y_m)$.

nodes.name: Weights, activation and width notation
nodes.statement: Here $p_{j} = {\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j)$, ${\bf{W}}_{m}$ is a matrix of weights for the $m^{th}$ layer, $g$ is the non-linear activation function, and $N$ is the number of nodes in the hidden layers respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Notation: $p_j$ the weighted input, $W_m$ the weight matrix, $g$ the activation, $N$ the layer width.

nodes.name: Gaussian i.i.d. weights
nodes.statement: The weights ${\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)$ are assumed to be independent identically distributed normal random variables with mean 0 and variance $v^{2}$.

nodes.name: i.i.d. standardized inputs
nodes.statement: Consistent with the assumptions in \cite{glorot2010understanding} and \cite{he2015delving}, I assume that the inputs to the first layer are independent and identically distributed random variables with mean 0 and variance 1.

nodes.name: Mean and variance of $y_{m}(i)$
nodes.statement: For convenience, I use $r_{m}$ and $u_{m}^{2}$ to denote the mean and variance of $y_{m}(i)$ respectively.

nodes.name: Layer input mean and variance $\mu_m$, $s_m^2$
nodes.statement: Due to the symmetry in the problem, all inputs to the $m^{th}$ layer will have the same means and variances during the first forward pass (i.e., $E(x_{m}(i)) = \mu_m$ and $Var(x_{m}(i)) = s_{m}^{2}$ for all $i$); the covariances between the inputs to the $m^{th}$ layer need not be 0.
nodes.statement_short: By symmetry all inputs of layer $m$ share mean $\mu_m$ and variance $s_m^2$ on the first forward pass.

nodes.name: Variance-preserving initialization problem
nodes.statement: The goal is to find the value of $v^{2}$ which ensures that $s_{1}^{2} \approx s_{2}^{2} ...\approx s_{M}^{2} = 1$ during the first forward pass.
nodes.statement_short: Find $v^2$ such that all layer-input variances $s_m^2$ stay about 1 on the first forward pass.

nodes.name: Pre-activation recursion
nodes.statement: y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N}{\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij} \enum{in1}
nodes.label: eq:in1

nodes.name: Activation recursion
nodes.statement: x_{m+1}(i) = \mbox{g}(y_{m}(i)). \enum{in2}
nodes.label: eq:in2

nodes.name: Independence of weights and layer inputs
nodes.statement: During the first iteration, $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ for all values of $i, j$ and $k$
conclusions: $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ for all values of $i, j$ and $k$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1
nodes.statement: Using the recursions in (\ref {eq:in1}) and (\ref {eq:in2}), $x_{m}(k)$ can be expressed as some non-linear function of the weights in the first $m-1$ layers, and the inputs to the first layer. Since the weights in the $m^{th}$ layer are independent of the inputs to the first layer and the weights in all other layers, the weights in the $m^{th}$ layer will also be independent of any non-linear function of these quantities. Therefore, $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ for all values of $i, j$ and $k$. Furthermore, since $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ and $x_{m}(l)$, $W_{m}(i,j)$ will also be independent of $x_{m}(k)x_{m}(l)$\qedsymbol
nodes.statement_short: $x_m$ is a function of earlier weights and inputs, which are independent of $W_m$.

nodes.name: Express $x_m$ via earlier layers
nodes.statement: Using the recursions in (\ref {eq:in1}) and (\ref {eq:in2}), $x_{m}(k)$ can be expressed as some non-linear function of the weights in the first $m-1$ layers, and the inputs to the first layer.
nodes.statement_short: Write $x_m(k)$ as a function of earlier weights and the first-layer inputs.

nodes.name: Independence of functions
nodes.statement: Since the weights in the $m^{th}$ layer are independent of the inputs to the first layer and the weights in all other layers, the weights in the $m^{th}$ layer will also be independent of any non-linear function of these quantities. Therefore, $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ for all values of $i, j$ and $k$.
nodes.statement_short: Weights of layer $m$ are independent of any function of those quantities, hence of $x_m(k)$.

nodes.name: Independence of products
nodes.statement: Furthermore, since $W_{m}(i,j)$ is independent of $x_{m}(k)$ and $x_{m}(l)$, $W_{m}(i,j)$ will also be independent of $x_{m}(k)x_{m}(l)$\qedsymbol
nodes.statement_short: Extend independence to products $x_m(k)x_m(l)$.

nodes.name: Zero mean of pre-activations
nodes.statement: r_{m} = E(y_{m}(i)) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j))E(x_{m}(j)) = 0. \enum{in201}
nodes.statement_short: $E(y_m(i))=0$ since weights have mean zero.
nodes.label: eq:in201

nodes.name: Expansion of the pre-activation variance
nodes.statement: \begin{split} u_{m}^{2} &= E\left(\sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N}{\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j)\right)^{2} \\ &= \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)^{2}x_{m}(j)^{2}\right) + 2\sum E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(k,l)x_{m}(l)\right). \\ \enum{in203} \end{split}
nodes.label: eq:in203

nodes.name: Pre-activation variance formula
nodes.statement: \begin{split} u_{m}^{2} &= \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)^{2}x_{m}(j)^{2}\right) \\ &= \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)^{2}\right)E\left(x_{m}(j)^{2}\right) \\ &= Nv^{2}(s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}) \\ \enum{in204} \end{split}
nodes.label: eq:in204

nodes.name: Variance formula holds for arbitrary input covariance
nodes.statement: Interestingly, this result holds for any arbitrary covariance structure of the inputs to the $m^{th}$ layer.

nodes.name: Large layer width
nodes.statement: To answer this question, I make the additional assumption that the number of nodes in the hidden layer ($N$) is `large'; this assumption is reasonable given that most neural networks have several hundred nodes in the hidden layers.

nodes.name: Approximate normality of pre-activations
nodes.statement: $y_{m}(i)$ will be approximately normally distributed for all values of $m$ and $i$.
assumptions: the number of nodes in the hidden layer ($N$) is `large'
conclusions: $y_{m}(i)$ will be approximately normally distributed for all values of $m$ and $i$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2
nodes.statement: For the first iteration, note that $E(p_{ij}) = E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j)\right) = E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)\right)E\left(x_{m}(j)\right) = 0$. Furthermore, for $j \neq k$, \begin{equation} \begin{split} Cov(p_{ij},p_{ik})&= E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) - E(p_{ij})E(p_{ik}) \\ &= E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) \\ &= E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(i,k)x_{m}(k)\right) = 0,\\ \end{split} \end{equation} where the last equality follows from (\ref {eq:in2041}). This implies that $p_{i1}$, $p_{i2}$ ... $p_{iN}$ are independent and identically distributed random variables. Therefore by the Central Limit Theorem, we expect $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ to converge to a normal distribution when $N$ is large \cite{lehmann2004elements}. Even when $p_{i1}$, $p_{i2}$ ... $p_{iN}$ are dependent and not identically distributed, the conditions required to ensure that $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ converges to a normal distribution are weak (for a list of all the conditions, see Theorem 2.8.2 in \cite{lehmann2004elements}). Thus, $y_{m}(i)$ is expected to to be approximately normally distributed during most iterations. \qedsymbol
nodes.statement_short: The summands $p_{ij}$ have mean 0 and are uncorrelated, so the Central Limit Theorem makes $y_m(i)$ approximately normal.

nodes.name: Zero mean of summands
nodes.statement: For the first iteration, note that $E(p_{ij}) = E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j)\right) = E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)\right)E\left(x_{m}(j)\right) = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: The summands $p_{ij}$ have mean zero.

nodes.name: Zero covariance of summands
nodes.statement: Furthermore, for $j \neq k$, \begin{equation} \begin{split} Cov(p_{ij},p_{ik})&= E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) - E(p_{ij})E(p_{ik}) \\ &= E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) \\ &= E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(i,k)x_{m}(k)\right) = 0,\\ \end{split} \end{equation} where the last equality follows from (\ref {eq:in2041}).
nodes.statement_short: The summands are pairwise uncorrelated, by (5).

nodes.name: Apply the Central Limit Theorem
nodes.statement: This implies that $p_{i1}$, $p_{i2}$ ... $p_{iN}$ are independent and identically distributed random variables. Therefore by the Central Limit Theorem, we expect $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ to converge to a normal distribution when $N$ is large \cite{lehmann2004elements}.
nodes.statement_short: Treat the summands as i.i.d. and apply the Central Limit Theorem.

nodes.name: Dependent summands
nodes.statement: Even when $p_{i1}$, $p_{i2}$ ... $p_{iN}$ are dependent and not identically distributed, the conditions required to ensure that $y_{m}(i) = \sum\limits_{j=1}^{j=N} p_{ij}$ converges to a normal distribution are weak (for a list of all the conditions, see Theorem 2.8.2 in \cite{lehmann2004elements}).
nodes.statement_short: Weak conditions give normality even for dependent, non-identical summands.

nodes.name: Conclude normality
nodes.statement: Thus, $y_{m}(i)$ is expected to to be approximately normally distributed during most iterations. \qedsymbol
nodes.statement_short: Conclude $y_m(i)$ is approximately normal.

nodes.name: Zero covariance of summands
nodes.statement: \begin{split} Cov(p_{ij},p_{ik})&= E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) - E(p_{ij})E(p_{ik}) \\ &= E(p_{ij}p_{ik}) \\ &= E\left({\bf{W}}_{m}(i,j)x_{m}(j){\bf{W}}_{m}(i,k)x_{m}(k)\right) = 0,\\ \end{split}

nodes.name: First-order Taylor linearization of the activation
nodes.statement: Assuming that the higher order terms can be ignored, \begin{equation} x_{m+1}(i) \approx g(0) + (y_{m} - 0)g'(0). \enum{in205} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Linearize $g$ about 0: $x_{m+1}(i)\approx g(0)+y_m g'(0)$.

nodes.name: Mean of next-layer inputs
nodes.statement: \mu_{m+1} = E(x_{m+1}(i)) \approx g(0). \enum{in206}
nodes.label: eq:in206

nodes.name: Constant layer-input mean
nodes.statement: \mu_{j} = g(0) \mbox{ for all } j\geq 1 \enum{in2061}.
nodes.statement_short: $\mu_j = g(0)$ for all layers.
nodes.label: eq:in2061

nodes.name: General weight initialization for differentiable activations
nodes.label: eq:in208

nodes.name: General initialization strategy for activations differentiable at 0
nodes.statement: Equation (\ref {eq:in208}) provide a general weight initialization strategy for any arbitrary differentiable activation function.
conclusions: Equation (\ref {eq:in208}) provide a general weight initialization strategy for any arbitrary differentiable activation function.
nodes.statement_short: For any activation differentiable at 0, use $v^2 = 1/(N g'(0)^2 (1+g(0)^2))$.

nodes.name: Hyperbolic tangent activation
nodes.statement: g(x) =\mbox{tanh}(x),

nodes.name: Tanh initialization equals Xavier initialization
nodes.statement: Plugging these results in (\ref {eq:in208}) yields \begin{equation} v \approx \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}, \enum{tanh1} \end{equation} which is precisely the {\it{Xavier Initialization}}.
nodes.statement_short: For tanh ($g(0)=0$, $g'(0)=1$) the general rule gives $v\approx 1/\sqrt N$, the Xavier initialization.

nodes.name: Tanh initialization
nodes.statement: v \approx \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}, \enum{tanh1}
nodes.label: eq:tanh1

nodes.name: Sequential saturation of tanh layers
nodes.statement: In their analysis of a neural network with the hyperbolic tangent activations, \cite{glorot2010understanding} find that the deeper layers in the neural network have a greater proportion of unsaturated nodes than the shallower layers. As is stated in their paper, `why this is happening remains to be understood'.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent
nodes.statement_short: Why deeper tanh layers have more unsaturated nodes than shallower ones was left unexplained.

nodes.name: Explanation of sequential saturation
nodes.statement: To explain their finding, I begin by noting that in \cite{glorot2010understanding}, the authors initialize the weights using samples from a uniform distribution $\left(U[-1/\sqrt{N},1/\sqrt{N}]\right)$ having a variance of $1/3N$. Therefore, from (\ref {eq:in2061}) and (\ref {eq:in207}), with $g(0) = 0$ and $g'(0) = 1$, we have $\mu_{m} = 0$ and \begin{equation} s_{m+1}^{2} = \frac{1}{3}s_{m}^{2} < s_{m}^{2} \end{equation} \enum{seq1} respectively. From (\ref {eq:in204}), this implies that $u_{m+1}^{2}<u_{m}^{2}$ for all $m$ (i.e., $u_{m}^{2}$ is a decreasing function of $m$). Furthermore from proposition 2, $y_{m}(i) \sim {\cal{N}}(0,u_{m}^{2})$. Therefore, $x_{m+1}(i)$ will be the tanh transformation of a normal random variable. Using results from \cite{godfrey2009tanh}, $x_{m+1}(i) = \mbox{tanh}(y_{m}(i))$ will have a probability density function (pdf) given by \begin{equation} f(y) = \frac{1}{1-y^{2}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi u_{m}^{2}}}\mbox{e}^{\left({-\frac{t_{y}^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}\right)} \enum{tanh1}, \end{equation} where \begin{equation} t_{y} = \frac{1}{2} ln\left(\frac{1+y}{1-y}\right). \end{equation} Plots of this pdf for different values of $u_{m}$ (provided in Figure \ref{fig:tanh}) produce trends similar to those observed by the simulation studies of \cite{glorot2010understanding} (figure 4 in their paper). A comparison of Figure \ref{fig:tanh} and figure 4 of \cite{glorot2010understanding} suggests that $u_{m}^{2}$ is a decreasing function of $m$, as is expected. From the results in \cite{godfrey2009tanh}, we expect the activations to be (a) approximately normally distributed when $u_{m}$ is close to 0 and (b) bimodally distributed with local maximas near -1 and +1 when $u_{m}$ is close to 1.
nodes.section: Sequential saturation with the hyperbolic tangent
nodes.statement_short: Uniform initialization gives variance $1/3N$, so $u_m^2$ decreases with depth; the tanh of a normal is bimodal for large $u_m$.

nodes.statement: Furthermore from proposition 2, $y_{m}(i) \sim {\cal{N}}(0,u_{m}^{2})$. Therefore, $x_{m+1}(i)$ will be the tanh transformation of a normal random variable.

A comparison of Figure \ref{fig:tanh} and figure 4 of \cite{glorot2010understanding} suggests that $u_{m}^{2}$ is a decreasing function of $m$, as is expected.

nodes.statement: From the results in \cite{godfrey2009tanh}, we expect the activations to be (a) approximately normally distributed when $u_{m}$ is close to 0 and (b) bimodally distributed with local maximas near -1 and +1 when $u_{m}$ is close to 1.

nodes.statement_short: Activations are near-normal for small $u_m$ and bimodal near $\pm1$ for $u_m$ near 1.

nodes.name: Shallower tanh layers saturate more
nodes.statement: Accordingly, since $u_{m}^{2}$ is a decreasing function of $m$, we expect the activations from the shallower layers to be more saturated (i.e., more concentrated near -1 and +1), and the saturation in the activations to reduce as we go to the deeper layers in the network.

nodes.name: Sigmoid activation
nodes.statement: g(x) = \frac{1}{1 + \mbox{e}^{-x}}

nodes.name: Sigmoid initialization
nodes.statement: v \approx \frac{3.6}{\sqrt{N}}, \enum{relur}
nodes.statement_short: $v\approx 3.6/\sqrt N$ for the sigmoid.
nodes.label: eq:relur

nodes.name: Sigmoid initialization converges where Xavier stalls
nodes.statement: A comparison of the validation accuracies for the 2 cases is provided in Figure \ref{fig:conv}, which shows that the convergence appears to stall with the {\it{Xavier initialization}}, but proceeds rapidly with the initialization proposed in (\ref {eq:relur}).
conclusions: the convergence appears to stall with the {\it{Xavier initialization}}, but proceeds rapidly with the initialization proposed in (\ref {eq:relur})
nodes.statement_short: On CIFAR-10 a 10-layer sigmoid network stalls with Xavier but converges with $v\approx3.6/\sqrt N$.

nodes.name: Derivation of the RELU initialization
nodes.statement: Since the RELU activation is not differentiable at 0, the results from ({\ref{eq:in205}}~--~{\ref{eq:in207}}) cannot be used to compute the optimal value of $v^{2}$. To proceed, I use proposition 2 and (\ref {eq:in201}) which state that for the first iteration, $ y_{m}(i) \sim {\cal{N}}(0,u_{m}^{2})$. We are interested in in the mean and variance of $x_{m+1}(i) = \mbox{max}(0,y_{m}(i))$. The mean will be given by \begin{equation} \mu_{m+1} = E(y_{m}(i){\bf{I}}(y_{m}(i)>0)) = \frac{1}{{u_{m}\sqrt{2\pi}}}\int_{0}^{\infty} x \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}dx = \frac{u_{m}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\mbox{e}^{-t}dt = \frac{u_{m}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}. \enum{relu1} \end{equation} Similarly, \begin{equation} E(x_{m+1}(i)^{2}) = \frac{1}{{u_{m}\sqrt{2\pi}}}\int_{0}^{\infty} x^{2} \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}dx = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \frac{1}{{u\sqrt{2\pi}}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x^{2} \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u^{2}}}dx = \frac{u_{m}^{2}}{2}. \enum{relu2} \end{equation} Using (\ref {eq:relu1}) and (\ref {eq:relu2}), \begin{equation} s_{m+1}^{2} = E(x_{m+1}(i)^{2}) - \mu_{m+1}^{2} = \frac{u_{m}^{2}}{2} - \frac{u_{m}^{2}}{2\pi} \approx 0.34u_{m}^{2}. \enum{relu3} \end{equation} For the variance to be maintained at each iteration, we require $s_{m+1}^{2} \approx 1$ which yields \begin{equation} u_{m}^{2} \approx 3. \enum{relu301} \end{equation} Plugging (\ref {eq:relu301}) in (\ref {eq:relu1}) yields $\mu_{m+1} \approx 0.7$. By the symmetry of the problem during the first iteration, we expect $\mu_{m+1} \approx \mu_{m} ... \approx \mu_{2} \approx 0.7$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute mean and second moment of a rectified normal, require unit variance to get $u_m^2\approx3$, $\mu\approx0.7$.

nodes.name: Pre-activations are centred normal
nodes.statement: Since the RELU activation is not differentiable at 0, the results from ({\ref{eq:in205}}~--~{\ref{eq:in207}}) cannot be used to compute the optimal value of $v^{2}$. To proceed, I use proposition 2 and (\ref {eq:in201}) which state that for the first iteration, $ y_{m}(i) \sim {\cal{N}}(0,u_{m}^{2})$.
nodes.statement_short: Taylor approach fails; use Proposition 2 and (3): $y_m(i)\sim N(0,u_m^2)$.

nodes.name: Mean of rectified normal
nodes.statement: We are interested in in the mean and variance of $x_{m+1}(i) = \mbox{max}(0,y_{m}(i))$. The mean will be given by \begin{equation} \mu_{m+1} = E(y_{m}(i){\bf{I}}(y_{m}(i)>0)) = \frac{1}{{u_{m}\sqrt{2\pi}}}\int_{0}^{\infty} x \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}dx = \frac{u_{m}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\mbox{e}^{-t}dt = \frac{u_{m}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}. \enum{relu1} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Integrate to get $\mu_{m+1}=u_m/\sqrt{2\pi}$.

nodes.name: Second moment of rectified normal
nodes.statement: Similarly, \begin{equation} E(x_{m+1}(i)^{2}) = \frac{1}{{u_{m}\sqrt{2\pi}}}\int_{0}^{\infty} x^{2} \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u_{m}^{2}}}dx = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) \frac{1}{{u\sqrt{2\pi}}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x^{2} \mbox{e}^{-\frac{x^{2}}{2u^{2}}}dx = \frac{u_{m}^{2}}{2}. \enum{relu2} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Second moment is $u_m^2/2$.

nodes.name: Variance of rectified normal
nodes.statement: Using (\ref {eq:relu1}) and (\ref {eq:relu2}), \begin{equation} s_{m+1}^{2} = E(x_{m+1}(i)^{2}) - \mu_{m+1}^{2} = \frac{u_{m}^{2}}{2} - \frac{u_{m}^{2}}{2\pi} \approx 0.34u_{m}^{2}. \enum{relu3} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Variance is about $0.34 u_m^2$.

nodes.name: Unit-variance requirement
nodes.statement: For the variance to be maintained at each iteration, we require $s_{m+1}^{2} \approx 1$ which yields \begin{equation} u_{m}^{2} \approx 3. \enum{relu301} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Requiring $s_{m+1}^2\approx1$ gives $u_m^2\approx3$.

nodes.name: Layer means

nodes.statement_short: Hence $\mu_m\approx0.7$ for all layers.

nodes.statement: To understand why this happens, I compute the central moments of $x_{m+1}$ in terms of the central moments of $x_{m}$ when $v^{2} = 1/N$. From (\ref {eq:in204}) we have \begin{equation} u_{m}^{2} = s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}. \enum{r01} \end{equation} Plugging results from (\ref {eq:r01}) into (\ref {eq:relu1}) yields the recursion \begin{equation} \mu_{m+1}^{2} = \frac{1}{2\pi}(s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}) \approx 0.16(s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}). \enum{r02} \end{equation} Similarly, plugging results from (\ref {eq:r01}) and (\ref {eq:r02}) in (\ref {eq:relu3}) yields \begin{equation} s_{m+1}^{2} \approx 0.34(s_{m}^{2} + \mu_{m}^{2}). \enum{relu5} \end{equation} Simple manipulations of equations ({\ref{eq:r01}}~--~{\ref{eq:relu5}}) gives \begin{equation} \mu_{m}^{2} \approx 0.16 \times (0.51)^{m-1} \enum{relu603} \end{equation} and \begin{equation} s_{m}^{2} \approx 0.34 \times (0.51)^{m-1}. \enum{relu602} \end{equation} for all $m \geq 1$.

nodes.name: Xavier initialization degrades with depth for RELU
nodes.statement: Equation (\ref {eq:relu602}) shows that the variance of the inputs to the deeper layers is exponentially smaller than the variance of the inputs to the shallower layer. Therefore, the deeper the neural network, the worse the performance of the {\it{Xavier Initialization}} will be.

nodes.name: Variance gap between 22 and 30 layers
nodes.statement: From (\ref {eq:relu602}), $s_{22}^{2} \approx 1.62 \times 10^{-7}$ and $s_{30}^{2} \approx 6.33 \times 10^{-10}$. Thus the variance in the input to the $30^{th}$ layer will be $(0.51)^{8} = 3 \times 10^{-3}$ times smaller than the variance to the $22^{nd}$ layer, and explains the possible reason why the 30 layer neural network described in \cite{he2015delving} converges, but the 22 layer neural network does not.

nodes.statement_short: The 30th-layer variance is $0.51^8\approx3\times10^{-3}$ times the 22nd's, explaining the different convergence.
